title: Introduction & Scope
shortExplanation: The Banking Offence and Punishment Act, 2064 (2008) was enacted to consolidate and amend laws relating to banking offences in Nepal. It defines what constitutes a banking offence, prescribes penalties, and establishes adjudication mechanisms. The Act applies to all banks and financial institutions licensed by Nepal Rastra Bank. Prior to this Act, banking offences were scattered across multiple laws, making prosecution difficult. This Act streamlined the process and introduced stricter penalties to deter financial crimes. Understanding its scope is essential for bankers, auditors, and legal professionals working in the financial sector.
q1_text: What year was the Banking Offence and Punishment Act enacted?
q1_explanation: The Act was enacted in 2064 BS (2008 AD), replacing older scattered provisions across the Banking Act and other laws. It created a unified legal framework specifically targeting banking offences.
q2_text: Who does this Act apply to?
q2_optionA: All NRB-licensed banks and financial institutions
q2_explanation: The Act applies to all banks and financial institutions licensed by Nepal Rastra Bank, including commercial banks, development banks, finance companies, and microfinance institutions.
q3_text: What was the main reason for enacting this Act?
q3_optionA: To consolidate scattered banking offence laws
q3_explanation: Before this Act, banking offences were covered under multiple laws. The consolidation made investigation, prosecution, and adjudication more efficient and effective.

title: Definition of Banking Offences
shortExplanation: Section 3 of the Act defines a banking offence as any act or omission that contravenes the provisions of the Act or directives issued under it. Specific offences include fraud, forgery, misappropriation of funds, unauthorized lending, and knowingly presenting false financial information. The Act distinguishes between criminal offences (involving mens rea or guilty intention) and regulatory violations (strict liability). Criminal offences carry imprisonment terms, while regulatory violations attract monetary penalties. This distinction is crucial for bankers to understand when reporting suspicious activities to NRB and law enforcement agencies.
q1_text: What is required for a criminal banking offence?
q1_explanation: Criminal banking offences require mens rea — a guilty mind or intention to commit the wrongful act. Without proven intention, the act may only be a regulatory violation.
q2_text: What distinguishes a regulatory violation from a criminal offence?
q2_optionA: Regulatory violations attract only monetary penalties
q2_explanation: Regulatory violations (strict liability) attract monetary penalties only, while criminal offences require proven intent and carry imprisonment terms up to 15 years depending on the offence.
q3_text: Which of the following is NOT a banking offence under the Act?
q3_explanation: While late return submission may attract regulatory action under other directives, it is not classified as a banking offence under this Act. Fraud, forgery, and misappropriation are explicitly listed as banking offences.

title: Fraud by Directors and Employees
shortExplanation: Section 4 deals with fraud committed by directors, chief executive officers, and employees of financial institutions. The Act prescribes penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment and fines up to Rs. 500,000 for knowingly presenting false financial statements, concealing losses, or misrepresenting the institution's financial position. Directors who approve loans without proper due diligence or for personal benefit are also liable. The burden of proof shifts in certain cases where the director had a fiduciary duty to disclose. This section aims to ensure transparency in financial reporting and accountability at the highest levels of management.
q1_text: What is the maximum imprisonment for director fraud?
q1_explanation: Section 4 prescribes up to 10 years imprisonment for directors convicted of fraud, plus fines up to Rs. 500,000. The penalty reflects the serious breach of fiduciary duty.
q2_text: What must be proven for a director to be liable?
q2_explanation: Liability requires knowledge — the director must have knowingly presented false information or concealed losses. Negligence alone is insufficient for criminal liability under this section.
q3_text: What additional liability can directors face for loans?
q3_optionB: Approving loans with good interest rates
q3_explanation: Directors who approve loans without proper due diligence or for personal benefit are personally liable. NRB's Unified Directives further require directors to exercise the same care as a prudent person would in similar circumstances.

title: Forgery and Document Offences
shortExplanation: Forgery of bank documents carries severe penalties under Section 5 of the Act. Knowingly making or possessing a false document with intent to cause harm or gain advantage carries up to 10 years imprisonment and fines up to Rs. 500,000. This includes forged cheques, demand drafts, letters of credit, fixed deposit receipts, and loan agreements. The act of forgery is considered complete once the false document is created with fraudulent intent, regardless of whether any financial loss actually occurred. Banks must have robust document verification systems and staff training to detect forgeries early.
q1_text: What is required for forgery to be complete?
q1_optionA: Creation of false document with fraudulent intent
q1_explanation: Forgery is complete upon creation of the false document with fraudulent intent. Actual loss is not required for prosecution. The act punishes the intent and the act of forgery itself.
q2_text: What is the maximum penalty for cheque forgery?
q2_explanation: Cheque forgery carries the same penalty as other document forgeries under Section 5 — up to 10 years and fine up to Rs. 500,000. The severity reflects the potential for large-scale financial damage.
q3_text: What should banks implement to detect forgeries?
q3_explanation: Banks must implement document verification systems, train staff on detecting forged documents, and use secure printing technologies for negotiable instruments to prevent and detect forgeries.

title: Adjudication Process
shortExplanation: The Act establishes a special adjudication process for banking offences through Banking Offence Tribunals. Each tribunal consists of a District Judge as Chairperson and two members with banking expertise. The tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to try banking offences. Cases are initiated through the Public Prosecutor's office upon recommendation from NRB. The tribunal follows summary procedure for faster resolution. Appeals against tribunal decisions lie with the High Court within 35 days. This specialized mechanism ensures that banking offences are handled by experts who understand both legal principles and banking practices.
q1_text: How many members sit on a Banking Offence Tribunal?
q1_explanation: The tribunal comprises a District Judge as Chairperson and two members with banking expertise. This ensures both legal rigor and banking domain knowledge in adjudication.
q2_text: Which court hears appeals from Banking Offence Tribunals?
q2_explanation: Appeals against Banking Offence Tribunal decisions lie with the High Court and must be filed within 35 days of the tribunal's decision. The High Court reviews both questions of law and fact.
q3_text: Who initiates cases at the tribunal?
q3_optionB: The bank directly files a case
q3_explanation: Cases are initiated by the Public Prosecutor's office upon recommendation from NRB. This ensures that only cases with sufficient evidence and regulatory merit proceed to trial.

title: Adjudication Process — Trial Procedure
shortExplanation: The Banking Offence Tribunal follows a summary procedure designed for expedited resolution. The accused is served with a notice within 7 days of case registration. Evidence must be submitted within 30 days, and the tribunal aims to conclude trials within 90 days. The tribunal has powers equivalent to a civil court for summoning witnesses, requiring document production, and administering oaths. Legal representation is permitted, and the accused has the right to defend themselves. The summary procedure balances the need for swift justice with fundamental fair trial rights.
q1_text: What is the maximum timeframe for trial conclusion?
q1_explanation: The Act aims to conclude trials within 90 days of registration. This summary procedure is much faster than regular court proceedings, reflecting the urgency of banking offence adjudication.
q2_text: What powers does the tribunal have?
q2_optionA: Powers equivalent to a civil court
q2_explanation: The tribunal has powers equivalent to a civil court including summoning witnesses, requiring document production, examining evidence under oath, and ordering document disclosure.
q3_text: When must the accused be served notice?
q3_explanation: The accused must be served notice within 7 days of case registration at the tribunal. This ensures the accused has adequate time to prepare their defense within the summary timeline.

title: Adjudication Process — Penalties
shortExplanation: Upon conviction, the tribunal imposes penalties as prescribed by the Act. Imprisonment terms range from 6 months to 15 years depending on the offence. Fines range from Rs. 100,000 to Rs. 500,000 or the amount involved in the offence, whichever is higher. The tribunal may also order restitution — requiring the convicted person to repay the misappropriated amount to the financial institution. For regulatory violations without criminal intent, monetary penalties apply. Repeat offenders face enhanced penalties up to double the maximum prescribed for the first offence. All penalties must be deposited in the government treasury within the timeframe specified by the tribunal.
q1_text: What is the imprisonment range under the Act?
q1_explanation: The Act prescribes imprisonment from 6 months (minimum) up to 15 years (maximum for serious offences like large-scale fraud). The tribunal determines the exact term based on offence severity.
q2_text: What additional order can the tribunal make beyond imprisonment and fines?
q2_explanation: The tribunal may order restitution, requiring the convicted person to repay the misappropriated amount to the financial institution. This ensures the institution recovers its losses.
q3_text: What penalty applies to repeat offenders?
q3_optionA: Up to double the maximum for first offence
q3_explanation: Repeat offenders face enhanced penalties up to double the maximum prescribed for the first offence. This acts as a strong deterrent against habitual banking offenders.

title: Introduction to Working Capital
shortExplanation: Working capital is the difference between a company's current assets and current liabilities. Under NRB Working Capital Guidelines 2027, banks must assess borrower's working capital cycle, liquidity position, and operating cycle before sanctioning limits. This module introduces the core concept and its importance in credit risk assessment. A proper understanding of working capital helps bankers evaluate the borrower's ability to meet short-term obligations and fund day-to-day operations efficiently.
q1_text: What is the formula for working capital?
q1_explanation: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. This measures a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using its short-term assets. A positive figure indicates the company can fund its operations and has buffer for unexpected expenses.
q2_text: Which body regulates working capital lending in Nepal?
q2_explanation: Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) issues directives for working capital lending under the Unified Directives. The latest update incorporates risk-based lending norms and sector-specific exposure limits that banks must follow when sanctioning working capital facilities.
q3_explanation: Positive working capital means current assets exceed current liabilities. This gives the company liquidity to fund operations, pay suppliers, and manage seasonal fluctuations without relying on external borrowing.

title: Classification of Working Capital Loans
shortExplanation: NRB classifies working capital loans into Overdraft (OD) and Cash Credit (CC). OD offers a flexible limit with interest charged only on drawn amount — ideal for seasonal needs. CC is a limit against hypothecation of inventory and receivables. Banks must classify based on business cycle, repayment capacity, and nature of working capital gap. Misclassification can lead to NPA and regulatory penalties under NRB directives.
q1_optionA: Flexible limit with interest on drawn amount
q1_explanation: OD allows drawing up to a sanctioned limit; interest applies only on utilized amount. Best for temporary cash flow gaps and seasonal peaks. NRB mandates that OD limits must be reviewed annually based on actual utilization pattern.
q2_text: What secures a Cash Credit facility?
q2_explanation: CC is a working capital limit secured by hypothecation of current assets — stock, raw materials, and book debts. The borrower retains possession but the bank has a charge over these assets. NRB requires periodic stock audits for CC accounts above Rs. 10 million.
q3_text: Which facility suits seasonal working capital needs?
q3_explanation: Seasonal businesses benefit from OD's flexibility — draw when inventory builds up pre-season, repay when sales generate cash. This matches the actual cash flow cycle better than a fixed CC limit.
